#8242. How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

When I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm. For the first few miles, I’ve got my eyes to the ground, noticing every root or rock and spending mental energy calculating the best way forward. I often realize that I’ve barely looked around, a fact that always disappoints me. After all, I came for a view, not to analyze a trail.

But as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more important. Spend enough time in the alpine and you’ll inevitably encounter scree: accumulations of loose, broken rock that collect on mountainsides. Even a well-placed foot can send a small wave of rock downhill. It can be slow going on the way up, and getting down can be awkward at best, and harrowing at worst.

But, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful. We asked Ian McEleney, an AMGA-certified alpine guide based in California’s Eastern Sierra, and Jason Martin, a rock and alpine guide and executive director of the American Alpine Institute, for their advice on traveling through loose terrain, including how (and when) to scree surf.

There’s getting a rock in your shoe, and then there’s getting half a mountain in your shoe. If you anticipate spending much time on scree, a pair of ankle gaiters can be “worth their weight in gold,” Martin says.

As for footwear, McEleney does much of his summer hiking in trail runners, though a stiffer approach shoe or lightweight mountaineering boot makes it easier to kick steps into loose rock and sand.

Perhaps the most useful piece of equipment is a pair of trekking poles. Both guides use them when traveling through scree fields. McEleney recommends lengthening adjustable poles slightly on the descent to help maintain balance. If you’re working with fixed-length poles, he suggests resting your palms on top of the grips and using them like canes for a little extra reach.

Scree crossings require much more attention than walking on your standard, well-maintained trail. It’s important to make sure you have the mental bandwidth before heading into loose terrain. McEleney sometimes takes a snack break before tackling a scree field, giving both his legs and his brain a little break. Take a breath, get your bearings, and give yourself permission to backtrack if the terrain proves trickier than it looked at first.

Before stepping onto a slope, take stock of what’s both above and below you. Are there other hikers who might send rocks tumbling your way? Is there a cliff band below you? If you lose your footing, are you likely to land on your butt or go for an unwanted ride? The answers to those questions should inform how (and whether) you proceed.

Loose rock comes in all shapes and sizes. “You can have marbles, baseballs, basketballs, beach balls and bigger on any slope,” Martin says. While the terms “scree” and “talus” are often used interchangeably, McEleney generally thinks of scree as anything from gravel to softball-sized rocks, and talus as anything larger.

“When I’m crossing a scree field, my default expectation is that each footstep will move,” McEleney says. Even seemingly stable boulder fields warrant extra care. Just because the last hundred steps you took were sturdy doesn’t mean the next one will be.

When descending a slope of soft, loose scree, McEleney borrows a technique from mountaineering: the plunge step, commonly used to descend soft snow. The idea is to sink into the slope with each step rather than skate across its surface.

With your trekking poles lengthened slightly, lift the toes of your leading foot as if you were doing the opposite of stepping on the gas pedal. Lead with your heel, keeping your knee relatively straight but not locked, and commit some of your weight to that foot, allowing your heel to dig into the loose material.

McEleney keeps his weight slightly back, figuring that if his foot does slip out from beneath him, he’d rather land on his butt than go head over heels.

Keep an eye on the consistency of the rock ahead of you, too. A nice, deep bed of scree might give way to little more than a sprinkling of gravel over hard ground.

You might think it’s best to give your hiking partners some extra space when traveling through scree, but both guides recommend the opposite. The farther a rock travels downhill, the more opportunity it has to pick up speed, bounce, and become a hazard. McEleney likes to keep his groups “conversationally close.”

“It drives me nuts to see ‘a leader’ way out ahead uphill in loose terrain,” Martin says. “It feels like they’re putting everyone at risk.”

It comes back to that situational awareness: being mindful of who’s in your fall line, whether that’s someone in your own hiking party or a stranger farther down the mountain. Avoid positioning yourselves directly above one another where possible, and recognize that exposed terrain or active rockfall may need a different way forward.

Ascending on scree can be, as McEleney puts it, a little “soul-destroying.” As tempting as it might be to rush through it, picking up the pace rarely does you any favors.

Rather than heading straight up a scree field, look for a way to link patches of larger, more stable rock, or take a switchbacking approach where there isn’t an established trail and you can avoid damaging vegetation. Martin also looks for well-traveled tracks through smaller rocks, where previous foot traffic might have compressed some of the loose material. If there’s an established trail through the scree, stick to it.

In softer scree, McEleney sometimes kicks steps into the slope, either to uncover more stable ground beneath the loose rock or to give his hiking partners a series of footsteps to follow.

And before resigning yourself to a particularly miserable slog, take another look around. Is there a way to skirt the scree field altogether, or to intercept it higher up the mountainside? Sometimes the easiest way up a scree field is to spend as little time on it as possible. Sometimes, it’s better to slide down and around.

Unlike plunge stepping, where you’re trying to dig your heel into the mountainside with each step, scree surfing (sometimes called scree skiing) involves intentionally sliding with the loose rock beneath your feet.

“The whole slope wants to go downhill anyway,” McEleney says. “You can just sort of ride it.”

On a slope of fine scree with a safe runout and nobody below you, start by taking a few deliberate downhill steps. You may find that the rock continues to move beneath your foot after you’ve planted it. Get comfortable with that sensation before attempting to intentionally slide. McEleney considers the first 50 to 100 feet an “information gathering phase,” during which he gets a feel for how much the material moves beneath him.

When surfing, McEleney likens his stance to that of a telemark skier. He keeps his feet about shoulder-width apart, one slightly ahead of the other, in what he describes as an “athletic stance,” allowing him to react as the rock shifts beneath him.

On particularly fine, deep scree, McEleney sometimes takes little bounding steps. Rather than trying to find a stationary foothold with each step, you’re allowing the mountain to carry you a little farther downhill. Keep your trekking poles handy for balance, prioritize control over speed, and pay particular attention to any changes in the size or depth of the rock ahead of you.

Not all scree is surfable, though, and not all guides are particularly fond of the technique.

“I’m not afraid of a standing glissade on snow, but I’m pretty worried about scree skiing,” Martin says. “I never feel like I have that much control.”

Martin feels more in control on softer, lower-angle slopes. A thin layer of gravel over hard ground, for instance, is considerably less forgiving than a deep bed of loose rock.

If you’re shouldering a particularly big pack or nearing the end of a long day, McEleney recommends taking a more conservative approach. If the terrain is unforgiving, your legs are shot, or you’re unsure of your ability to control a slide, there’s no shame in picking your way down the mountainside.

But if you do decide to send it, it’s a blast. For once, those little rocks that robbed you of your hard-earned elevation on the way up are working in your favor. Enjoy it: You can empty your shoes at the trailhead.

#8241. Cut Off for 6 Years, Denali’s Only Road and Its Wildest Country Are Reopen for 2027

The single road in Denali National Park winds through the heart of the park and ends in the remote historic mining town of Kantishna. Hikers and cyclists are now able to cross the newly completed Pretty Rocks Bridge, and full public park bus service is set to resume in 2027. (Photo: Pursuit)

“Bear! On the left!” I jolt forward from the front passenger seat to find where our driver has spotted a grizzly on the open tundra. On a steep slope covered with birch trees, pops of autumn amber and rust scattered against green spruce trees, I can make out a moving boulder—then I spot its golden blonde fur. Olivia Juarez, general manager of Denali Backcountry Lodge, tells me it’s the signature coat of Denali grizzlies. Juarez is driving three of us, including her dog, on the entire 92-mile nearly unpaved stretch of the Denali Park Road, which feels precarious at times due to two-thirds of it being only one lane. But the speed limit is 35 mph, and we are the only ones on it.

For the last six years, this mostly gravel mountain corridor—the only road through Denali National Park and Preserve—has been closed after mile 43 due to a landslide. But in time for the 2027 summer season, access to the full 92 miles will reopen, allowing visitors to explore the depths of Denali’s backcountry once again.

Juarez slows the van to a stop, and we pass around binoculars. The grizzly is far in the distance, but it’s what surrounds it in every direction that catches my breath: striking volcanic cliffs in a kaleidoscope of earthy hues and gravelly, braided glacial streams stretching across an endless expanse of wild. It’s only us on the road, and this grizzly out yonder, for as far as we can see. And out there, somewhere hidden under a cloak of clouds, is Denali, or The Great One, as the peak’s traditional name translates from the Koyukon Athabascan language.

On September 2, 2026, the long-awaited Pretty Rocks Bridge in Denali National Park was completed, an architectural marvel that bypasses the still-active landslide. At 475 feet long and 24 feet wide, the steel single-span truss bridge is just wide enough for a park bus to drive through.

This $230 million federal project includes 23 underground thermosiphons—a passive cooling technology that pulls heat out of the earth to keep the permafrost frozen year-round. Pedestrians and cyclists are currently permitted to cross, with full bus and vehicle service scheduled to resume in 2027.

I’ve spent the last four nights at Denali Backcountry Lodge, a remote all-inclusive outpost that sits at the end of the road. I flew in via a 45-mile helicopter ride, the only way guests can reach the property since the landslide. The lodge is the farthest place you can stay and still be in the park. We spent our days hiking through the spongy tundra, exploring the history of the Kantishna mining camp, and kayaking Wonder Lake with Denali in the background, a coveted sight since it was photographed by Ansel Adams on a rare cloudless day in 1947.

Since the road closure, no one other than guests staying at the three remote wilderness lodges has been able to visit these iconic areas of the park. While Denali Backcountry Lodge offers a chance to truly settle into the wild, all the excitement is found along the road. That is, nearly all our wildlife sightings (except for a grizzly sitting atop its moose kill spotted in the distance on one of our guided hikes) happened on a drive: a trio of caribou running, a moose moving through the willow marshes, a porcupine waddling across the road, a bear cub prancing out from the shrubs.

Starting in 2027, visitors will finally be able to reach the end of the road again on a Denali park bus. Guests staying at Denali Backcountry Lodge will arrive and depart via a private bus next year, and their Creekside Cabins guests will take a private bus in and fly out on a single-engine bush plane. Day guests will be able to reach the end of the road and book a guided experience at Denali Backcountry Lodge.

More travelers returning to Denali’s backcountry means there’s more opportunity to transform them into stewards of this land. “Visiting a place like this is life-changing for people,” says Alexa Donahe, vice president and general manager of Pursuit’s Alaska Collection, which includes Denali Backcountry Lodge. “Day traffic allows for more people who don’t have the time or resources to have an immersive backcountry experience like this and to experience the depths of the wilderness for a day.”

Even with more visitors coming in by bus, it will still feel remote, says Donahe. There will be strict park (and lodge) restrictions to preserve the landscape and wildlife. For comparison, more than 4 million people visit 2.2-million-acre Yellowstone yearly, with easy road access for private cars. Only 500,000 people visit Denali each year, but at 6 million acres, the park is the size of Vermont.

Sure, there are more people gathering at the park entrance, where you’ll find a visitor center and the famous Denali sled dogs, but once you reach the dirt road, it feels as remote as ever.

Only about 30 percent of visitors to Denali National Park and Preserve get a completely clear view of the peak. An even smaller subset—fewer than ten percent—experience a completely cloud-free, base-to-summit view. Visitors who stay multiple days (such as four days in Kantishna) see the mountain at much higher rates, around 85 percent. Because the massive 20,310-foot peak creates its own local weather system, heavy cloud cover frequently obscures the summit, especially during the summer tourism season.

One morning at breakfast, a group of Natural Habitat guests wait out bad weather to depart. Their expedition leader Samantha Strauss shares with me her thoughts on the fully opened Denali. “For every person who comes out and sees this place, that’s one more person that cares about public lands. Especially right now, public lands are not promised to us,” she says. “Even if that means I have less square mileage allotted just to myself, even if that means I have to share this space with more people, it is a conservation win because it helps people create a connection to the landscape and have a stake in its future.”

I flew over Denali National Park in a helicopter and left on the Denali Park Road, just days after the Pretty Rocks Bridge bypassing the landslide was completed. Both ways gave me different perspectives on this vast expanse of raw wilderness.

While it was thrilling to soar over glaciers and peaks, it was seeing Denali from the ground, my eyes scanning the landscape for wildlife, moving through the changing early autumn hues, feeling the rush of brisk air as I rolled my window down to take a photo, that made me feel I was a part of it. The road is the center line of this wilderness, and it’s not only the best way to see Denali’s untamed backcountry and wildlife, but to feel its beating heart.

Backyard birds tapping on windows is a sometimes funny, sometimes infuriating part of fall. Here's why they do it, and how to stop the behaviour if needs be.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Folk have long discussed why backyard birds peck windows in fall, and once Google got involved, plenty more possible causes were added to the pile. Now research and observations from bird experts have revealed the real reasons behind this bizarre behaviour, and you may be surprised to learn what they are.

Some of the most common speculations about why birds tap windows include attempting to get your attention when it's time to refill feeders, impending bad news, small songbirds wanting to come into the warm, and a message from a passed loved one. Avian experts, however, have put forward reasons based on cold, hard data, and they provide a fascinating insight into fall bird behaviour.

Whether you find the tap-tap-tapping of your beneficial garden friends endearing or highly annoying, once you understand the real reasons avian experts say are behind window pecking, you can better support your garden birds in fall. Understanding the likely causes will also help you decide if should take action to stop the window tapping to save birds from harm, and save your sanity, too.

As temperatures decrease in fall, insects become more scarce, many birds are forced to forage for food in new areas. Because glass retains heat from the sun as well as windows allowing some of a home’s heat to escape, any tiny gaps in frames become welcoming nooks for insects to enter diapause (similar to hibernation) – and consequently, one of those spots hungry birds may favor. You might think modern windows don’t offer much space for critters to hole up in, but those drainage weep holes and sliding tracks provide plenty of opportunities. Spiders also use window corners to spin insect-catching webs and lay eggs, offering further protein-rich food to the bird buffet.

According to the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO), there’s a rise in birds pecking at windows for food in fall and winter, and in particular by the tit family which includes chickadees and titmice. The organisation also cites that birds may pick at traditional window putty as it’s made with fish or linseed oil, both a valuable source of energy in colder months.

Research carried out by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology found that the lower angle of sunlight hitting windows in fall significantly increases how reflective the glass is. Aside from birds having no concept of what a window is, our feathered friends see differently to us. Most birds have eyes on the sides of their heads to give them almost-360° vision, and while that’s highly useful for spotting potential predators, it means their forward vision isn’t as good as ours. So, reflections in windows are easily interpreted as extra habitat and when birds encounter the glass – which in fall, especially, can appear to them as an invisible barrier – they may peck at it repeatedly to investigate.

Fall is when juvenile birds disperse, and these inexperienced youngsters have a lot to learn about the world around them, and much spatial awareness still to develop. Data published by the American Bird Conservancy and the US Fish & Wildlife Service shows a strong rise in what they term ‘glass interactions’ in fall. While many of these will be window collisions caused by mirror-like glass and navigational error, some will be window pecking led by curiosity as birds investigate their surroundings.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

While territorial behaviour among most of our feathered friends peaks in spring, many resident birds claim their territory in fall, according to the National Audubon Society. Northern cardinals, non-migrating American robins, northern mockingbirds, towhees and bluebirds are all highly territorial through fall into winter. And there's a very good reason for this, because as summer broods disperse, thousands of juvenile birds search a new territory. In the face of this competition, existing populations fiercely defend their established territories – especially if it contains a valuable food source such as a garden shrub hung with berries birds love through winter!

With windows becoming mirror-like in the low fall sun, dominant birds can attack their own reflection, mistaking it for a competitor. So this is a common reason why birds tap windows in fall as well as spring.

Whether you have a towhee aggressively pecking at your patio doors or a chickadee tap-tapping your bedroom window at all hours, now you understand what’s behind this behaviour, you can do something about it. Gentle pecking for food harms neither bird nor human, so it’s safe to ignore this low-level behaviour. But more insistent pecking at a window, fighting imagined aggressors or attempting to break through an invisible barrier is not just highly annoying to us but harmful to birds, damaging beaks and wasting valuable energy.

Taking action to stop birds pecking windows involves making glass more visible, or keeping birds away from it in the first place. That means these solutions will also reduce the risk of feathered friends flying into windows and injuring themselves. By working out the likely reason behind a bird tapping on your window, you can choose the method that will be most effective.

Your first step to stop birds tapping windows is to move any houseplants away from windows that are being targeted. To a young bird, a windowsill full of greenery can look like inviting habitat or contribute to the illusion that this could be a continuation of their flightpath.

A quick and cheap solution if the targeted window opens is to shut a length of double-sided reflective bird scare tape like this from Amazon in it. When the tape blows in the wind, its holographic surface casts erratic patterns of ultraviolet light which most birds perceive as a threat. For resident birds in search of tasty insects, this may be enough for them to deem that window an unsafe zone.

While the go-to for making windows more visible to birds and preventing collisions is decals, they're only effective if the gaps between them are narrow enough. A few decals dotted about on a large window are next to useless as birds will likely perceive the areas between them as possible flightpaths, just as they do the gaps between branches in woodland.

A far simpler, more effective and still-stylish alternative is to create a grid of dots around 2 inches apart across the entire window. Use a white oil-based permanent marker like a Sharpie Medium Point Paint Marker, available from Amazon, and for a professional result, use a stencil template. You could make your own by punching holes in cardboard or save yourself the trouble with an Avi-Dot Bird Saver Window Stencil from Etsy.

Another effective way to help birds see house windows as a barrier is to stick on clear collision tape like CollidEscape, available from Amazon. To be effective against bird strikes, and therefore cut down on curious birds pecking at what they perceive as an invisible wall, you’ll need to position the tape in vertical or horizontal stripes with the edges no more than 2 inches apart. If you have feathered friends that often peck at a particular part of a window, this is a useful method as you can reduce the gap between strips here.

If a particular bird still persists in pecking at a window, creating a temporary cardboard barrier can help break the habit.

If you have a problem with a particularly territorial or bigger bird such as a woodpecker or seagull, a final resort is to fix a permanent deterrent near to the targeted window. Wind-powered metal spinners throw out unpredictable flashes of light, visually confusing birds to create an area they perceive as unsafe. Windmill spinners like these Stainless Steel Bird Deterrent Devices by Ebern Designs on Wayfair mean you don’t have to compromise on garden style.

Backyard birds need our support more than ever once fall turns to winter, whether that's preventing a bird bath freezing over to preserve their water supply, saving up kitchen scraps to feed feathered friends, or making sure smaller songbirds get a fair share of food. Now you understand why birds tap on windows in fall, you can decide whether or not to ignore the behaviour or take action for your and the bird's benefit.

#8236. Officials Are Hunting for the Lake Tahoe Tree Killer

A person remains at large after poisoning at least 28 mature pines in three separate incidents over four years (Photo: Rachid Dahnoun/Getty Images)

Authorities in Nevada are looking for a person who has been poisoning trees on the shores of Lake Tahoe. Since 2022, at least 28 pines have been harmed or destroyed, totaling $300,000 in damages, authorities said in a release.

Now, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office (WCSO) and other local organizations are offering a $147,000 bounty to catch the culprit.

“We take these crimes very seriously and will utilize every available resource to identify and apprehend the person or persons responsible,” Sheriff Darin Balaam said in a statement. “The destruction of mature trees in the Tahoe Basin and the environmental damage caused by these deliberate acts are unacceptable.

In an email to Outside, WCSO spokesperson Rachel Piccinini said the agency is continuing to investigate the crimes, which could result in felony charges.

“Our office has received numerous tips from the community, and we continue to encourage anyone with information that may assist in this investigation to contact our Detective Division,” Piccinini said.

Outside requested further information about whether the incidents pose a threat to people or pets recreating in the area. We will update this article if we receive a response.

The tree poisonings have occurred at Burnt Cedar Beach, a lakefront recreation complex in Incline Village, Nevada, along Lake Tahoe’s north shore. It’s also about a ten-minute drive from the community-owned Diamond Peak Ski Resort. Roughly 9,000 people live in Incline Village, but the area is a tourism hotspot in both winter and summer.

A person remains at large after poisoning at least 28 mature pines in three separate incidents over four years. Authorities say they believe the same person damaged all the trees. The suspect harmed the first six in 2022 and another six in 2024.

Most recently, on July 24, 2026, deputies responded to Burnt Cedar Beach after reports of a strong odor near the base of a large pine tree. The smell matched previous tree poisonings at the property. On August 2, deputies found another tree with a substance around the base; at the time, a trail camera captured a bright light near the area at 2 A.M.

At least 16 trees were damaged in 2026 as a result.

In some instances, someone poured the toxin directly over the tree’s base. In others, someone drilled holes near the roots and poured the substance in them.

Authorities say they have yet to identify the contaminant or determine why someone targeted the trees. They have collected soil samples and submitted them for testing. They hope to identify the substance used and determine whether the perpetrator used the same one in each incident.

WCSO asks anyone with information to call (775) 328-3001 and reference case number 26-4225.

#8235. Gary Colliver Was a “Big-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions)

Gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

Later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a new route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

To Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions said. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”

Colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management plan for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

“There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher said. Although that initial plan was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

As a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular big wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions said.

#8234. What Does Trail Magic Look Like Around the World? These 5 Stories Show Us

The snacks at the hut made Matt's day, despite the mucky conditions (Photo: Matt Jordan)

On the 2024 Highlander UAE, a multi-day 40-mile hike through the Hajar Mountains, I struggled far more than I had expected. The terrain was brutal, with steep descents over sharp, rocky granite tracks along the 6,345-foot Jebel Jais summit. My heavy pack weighed me down, and I could feel every stone beneath my boots. By day three, my two big toes hurt so much that on one challenging descent, I collapsed and couldn’t take another step.

That’s when a local Emirati man came walking up the trail behind me. He saw that I was struggling and stopped to pull out a roll of tape from his bag. Then, he peeled off my very stinky hiking socks without a second thought, taped up my toes, and bandaged my knees. He even carried my pack for several miles, guiding me down the remaining steep sections.

This stranger had no reason to go out of his way to help me, and I know I could not have finished that day without him. Hikers call this kind of experience “trail magic.” The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines the term as any instance of finding what you need most when you least expect it; experiencing something rare, extraordinary, or inspiring in nature, or encountering unexpected acts of generosity that restore one’s faith in humanity.

Trail magic is often associated with Appalachian Trail history from the early 1980s. However, after my experience in the UAE, I started wondering what it looks like elsewhere. So, here are five stories from other hikers who have experienced trail magic in one form or another around the world.

Matt Jordan, a hiking and backpacking guide with Intrepid Travel, was walking New Zealand’s 1,881-mile Te Araroa Trail southbound in 2023 when he hit the muddy Longwood Forest in Fiordland. After a miserable day of rain and bog, he pushed on toward Turnbull’s Hut, one of the last backcountry huts on that segment. He’d heard that sometimes, free supplies were stored there for hikers passing through. As he approached, he prayed it hadn’t already all been taken by the time he got there.

“Thankfully it hadn’t,” he says. When he opened the store area, he found a cache of goodies.

“A local man who hikes in supplies, hauls out trash, and maintains the hut about twice a month leaves coolers stocked with beer, soda, and candy bars,” Jordan says. Excitedly, he grabbed a drink, then promptly slipped in the mud and fell on his backside. After days of awful weather conditions, though, that didn’t stop him from laughing out loud.

“For me, the gesture was about more than a cold drink. It was a reminder of the generosity of strangers and the sense of community that makes long-distance hikes unforgettable worldwide.”

Meeta Singh Rao, a hiking guide in India, says some of her best trail magic came from shepherds who spend months in the high mountain pastures of the Indian Himalayas. In October 2022, she was leading a trek to Nawali Bugyal in Uttarakhand when the weather turned. Heavy rain began to fall, and strong winds blew. The mules carrying their gear were also lost, and camp was miles away.

The group came across a shepherd with his flock. He heard where they were headed, and offered them shelter in his channi, a mountain hut made of stone, mud, and plastic sheets. “When rainwater leaked through the roof, he walked out into the downpour to rearrange the plastic so we stayed dry,” says Rao.

When Rao offered to pay, the shepherd gently refused, saying they were his guests. “A couple with so little of their own opened their home to us, giving us a feeling of belonging in the mountains,” she adds.

Kaitlyn Bussell has walked four Caminos. But her second, the 62-mile Camino Inglés in September 2023 through Galicia, was particularly challenging. The rain was constant, few hostels and cafés were open in the fall, and she walked long stretches without seeing another pilgrim.

On the second day, wet and ready for a break, she ducked into the first bar she found for a café con leche and to charge her phone. When she went to pay, the young woman behind the counter told her the coffee was free and handed her some water, prayer cards and a small Camino keepsake.

“It was a small thing, but it came at exactly the right moment,” Bussell recalls. “After days of rain, it lifted my spirits and made me realize that this pilgrimage is as much about the people you meet as it is the miles you walk.”

On Japan’s Shikoku 88 Temples Pilgrimage route, Lauren Roerick and her brother were leaving one of the temples when she spotted a sign offering matcha tea ceremonies for pilgrims. They initially walked away unsure whether they would be intruding but returned and decided to try it anyway.

“A Japanese man welcomed us inside where two women in kimonos were preparing and serving matcha under his instruction,” adds Roerick. “To make us feel welcome, he called a friend and had her on speakerphone, translating the whole ceremony from Japanese into English.” Lauren and her brother learned about the tradition, tried making tea themselves, and ate small Japanese sweets.

“It was proof that trail magic isn’t always a bottle of water or a helping hand,” says Roerick. “Sometimes a stranger opens his door, works around a language barrier, and shares a bit of culture with people passing through.”

On a windy hike to Matterhorn Base Camp, Libera Pagano, tour director with EF Adventures, noticed an older woman struggling. The altitude made her dizzy, her legs were shaking, and her friend had walked far ahead. “I offered to sit with the woman while she rested behind a large rock and we started chatting,” says Pagano.

That’s when Pagano learned it was the woman’s 86th birthday, and the hike was a present she’d given herself. They stayed together, and when the woman felt ready, they walked slowly until they caught up with her companion. When the group met back at basecamp, the woman told Pagano that without her help, she would never have made it to the summit.

“I thought nothing of what I had done,” says Pagano. “But for that woman, it was the difference between giving up and fulfilling her birthday wish.”

I never learned the name of the man who bandaged my toes in the Hajar Mountains, and I probably never will. But I think about him whenever I struggle on a trail or see another hiker limping.

All these stories have one thing in common—human compassion. Sometimes that is stopping to help a stranger in need, sharing what little you have, or leaving a cache of supplies for a hiker you’ll probably never meet. These gestures don’t have to be grand or cost much, but they can make an enormous difference and are an easy thing to pay forward so everyone experiences a little magic outdoors.

A greenhouse is nice to have, but your winter crops can get by without one. A few simple, inexpensive tricks can help hardy vegetables survive through winter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Your greens look great on Sunday afternoon. Then a clear, still night pulls the temperature down hard, and by Monday morning the lettuce has gone dark and limp, and the chard leaves look soft and water-soaked. It's a rough way to lose a bed of winter vegetables you've been tending since late summer, especially when the forecast only mentioned a light frost.

Several of the cold-hardy winter vegetables keep producing through the colder months, and a greenhouse isn't required to help them along. Cheap covers and a little attention on cold evenings go a long way, and a good share of the materials are probably in the garage already.

A handful of frosty nights in November is a different problem from weeks of frozen ground. Light covers can usually handle the first. That second one takes layers – fabric over the plants, mulch over the soil, and sometimes a solid structure on top.

Row covers get sold as frost blankets or horticultural fleece, but it's the same thin spun fabric either way. Light, air, and rain get through. What it holds in is warmth rising from the soil overnight, usually enough to keep lettuce, spinach, kale, and Swiss chard a few degrees warmer than bare beds. Heavy 1.5-ounce (51g/m²) cover holds more heat. It also blocks about half the light, so keep it for cold snaps.

Heat leaks out at the edges, so the cover has to touch the ground all the way around. Boards, bricks, or smooth rocks hold it down. If it sags onto tender leaves, slide a few hoops under it (see section 3). A row or two fits under the Agfabric 1.2-ounce frost cloth from Home Depot, a 10-by-50-foot (3 by 15 m) roll.

Cut the bottom out of an empty gallon (3.8L) milk jug, and it'll turn into a mini DIY greenhouse for a young lettuce or spinach plant. Smaller seedlings will get by under a soda bottle. Shove the cut edge into the dirt and pile soil around it, or it'll likely end up in the neighbor's yard after the first windy night. Then check that no leaves press on the plastic.

Your jug's cap comes off, too. Sealed up, a jug warms fast on a sunny afternoon, and the seedling can overheat while you're still outside in a jacket. Lift the jugs off on mild, bright days and drop them back on at dusk. If you run short on jugs, reusable clear plastic bell cloches, like these Senwell cloches from Amazon, go on the same way. They come with metal ground stakes to keep them in place.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Bend flexible ½-inch (1.3 cm) PVC pipe or heavy wire into hoops about 4 feet (1.2 m) apart over a bed, then stretch frost fabric or clear greenhouse plastic across the top. One tunnel can shelter a whole raised bed or a long row of greens. A Haxnicks fleece tunnel from Walmart comes with the steel hoops already attached and stretches to about 10 feet (3 m).

So should it get fabric or plastic? Fabric is the low-fuss choice, since air moves through it and it can stay on for days. Plastic gets warmer in the daytime and sheds rain, but after dark it's no warmer than fabric. Closed plastic can cook the greens on a bright afternoon, so pull up a side or open the ends. Wet, heavy snow can flatten it, too. Snowy areas need sturdier hoops set closer together, plus a brush-off after each storm.

You can leave carrots, parsnips, and other root crops in the bed past fall. Heap straw or shredded leaves on the row, and many of them will keep until you want them. Soil under that pile doesn't freeze as deep or flip between frozen and thawed as often. Left in over winter, a parsnip is, honestly, a sweeter parsnip come spring. Dig the rest before they bolt.

Mulch only protects the soil, though – it won't keep exposed kale or chard leaves from freezing on a hard night, so pair it with a cover. Be picky about the straw, too. Hay and bargain bales can be full of weed seed. GardenStraw wheat straw mulch from Lowe's is filtered, with most of the seed screened out, in a 2-cubic-foot (57L) box.

An old storm window in the garage is halfway to a cold frame. Hinge it to the back of a bottomless wooden box, or right onto a raised bed. Inside, it can run 10 to 20°F (6 to 11°C) warmer than the open garden. Spinach, mâche, and winter lettuce do well in one. Backyard Discovery's cedar cold frame from Walmart has a lid that lifts on its own once the inside passes 70°F (21°C).

Glass is heavy and can break, so secure the pane firmly so a gust can't slam it, and sand any sharp edges. Windows painted before 1978 may also contain lead paint – not something you want flaking into a food bed. On sunny days, heat is the bigger risk, so prop the lid open. Tuck a sensor like this AcuRite wireless thermometer from Lowe's inside the frame, and check it from the house.

Pots give you an option a bed doesn't. Their weak spot is down in the roots. Those are usually far less cold-hardy than the leaves, and a pot doesn't give them much soil for cover, so a freeze reaches them faster than roots in the ground. Still, you can pick up a pot of parsley, kale, or salad greens and carry it somewhere better. Crowd them by a wall the wind doesn't hit and throw burlap or bubble wrap around the bunch.

Water them well the day before a hard freeze. Wet soil freezes more slowly than dry soil, it turns out. On the bitter nights, carry the smaller ones into an unheated garage or shed. Get them back out the next morning, or once that cold spell is over. Greens left in a dim garage for days can come out pale and leggy.

Kale, collards, spinach, parsley, and cabbage can take a lot. Frost under 28°F (-2°C) usually doesn't bother them, but when the forecast calls for low 20°s F (around -6°C), cover them anyway. Lettuce, Swiss chard, beets, and carrots aren't quite as tough. Damage can show up in the mid- to upper 20°s (about -4 to -2°C). Mâche is the odd one out among salad greens and holds up better than lettuce. Beans, peppers, and tomatoes can't take even a light frost.

These ratings aren't fixed, though. Two varieties of the same crop can differ in hardiness, and an established kale plant usually gets through a freeze in better shape than one transplanted last week. Plants that have had several weeks of slowly cooling weather also hold up better than ones hit by a hard freeze after a warm spell. Watch how long the cold lasts, not just how low it'll go.

A greenhouse would be nice, sure, but straw over the carrots, fabric over the kale, and a couple of milk jugs over the late lettuce will carry a garden a long way. Keep a frost blanket folded by the back door. The night the forecast suddenly drops, it'll be the first thing you reach for.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8232. The Forest Service Just Released Bigfoot Records Dating Back to the 1940s. Here’s What They Say.

Wilderness explorer C. Thomas Biscardi, who spent nearly a decade searching for Bigfoot, claimed he photographed the elusive creature during an expedition in Northern California (Photo: Bettmann/Getty Images)

In the 1940s, a man named Leo Kinney described in an informal written account a disturbing encounter along Petty Creek, a tributary of the Clark Fork River west of Missoula, Montana. At the time, he and three other hunters went into the woods to pack out a six-point bull elk they had shot down.

“On arriving where the elk was supposed to be lying, we found the entrails only, and in the snow coming to and leading away from the area was a large set of tracks,” Kinney wrote in his 1980 retelling.

At first, the men guessed a large bear had eaten the elk—but the tracks appeared in sets of two, and bears don’t tend to walk on their hind legs.

“Whatever it was had picked up the elk whole and clear off the ground,” Kinney continued.

The men followed the tracks for about a half-mile and, according to Kinney’s account, came across a felled log measuring three feet in diameter. They could see where the elk’s horns had been dragged across the snow and over the timber.

“At this point we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was,” Kinney wrote. “Though we didn’t confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs.”

The following year, another person, W.W. Schmitz, was hunting in a nearby area called Bills Creek when he found the same type of tracks, smelled a similarly strong odor, and also heard grunting noises.

Kinney’s story is one of three historical files the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) released on October 15, describing Bigfoot encounters in Washington, Oregon, and Montana. In a world rife with sasquatch hunters and Bigfoot believers, the newly unveiled reports are shedding light on a long-held conspiracy theory. The public can access the files through the USFS website.

About 70 miles away in Plains, Montana, locals described an equally bizarre Bigfoot encounter in a January 15, 2003, article published by the Clark Fork Valley Press. According to the story, around January 3, hundreds of large, human-like footprints appeared in fresh snow outside Jim Rohweder’s sawmill shop. His neighbor, Bob Mesing, reportedly measured the prints at 16.5 inches long and 8.5 inches wide, with visible toes, an arch, and a stride that spanned about five feet.

Mesing and Dean Peterson, a former Kalispell policeman, followed the tracks about 100 yards into the woods, where the trail eventually faded.

“I don’t know if I believe in the Bigfoot theory, but the tracks were right there,” Mesing reportedly said. “What else could it be?”

According to the Clark Fork Valley Press, the men did not contact authorities but had planned to give a sample to wildlife officials.

Mesing said he believed the visitor walked up to the shop and turned back, startled by a motion-sensor light. Peterson reportedly added that his dog barked around 3:40 A.M. that day, but he saw nothing.

Rohweder’s wife, Gladys, claimed to have seen a hairy, two-legged creature when the couple first moved to the area.

A June 16, 1982, account published by the U.S. Department of Agriculture took place in Umatilla National Forest, which hugs the southern border of Washington State and northern Oregon. In it, wildlife biologist Rodney Johnson reports that the agency asked him to investigate three sets of Bigfoot tracks and record the details of his trips.

The tracks were recorded in three locations of the Mill Creek Watershed, a 36.5-mile tributary of the Walla Walla River about 262 miles from Portland.

Site A contained six identifiable tracks going down a muddy trail for about 25 feet. Similar tracks were also seen at a second location near a bog, Site B, this time 18 prints spanning about 40 feet.

Johnson took photos and plaster casts of both sites, but skipped the third, citing terrain challenges.

“It is my opinion that the tracks observed at Site ‘A’ and Site ‘B’ along Low Creek were made by something other than a 300-pound-plus two-footed being,” Johnson wrote.

When a two-legged being walks, its stride changes with gradient—shorter uphill and longer downhill. According to Johnson, the distance between the tracks remained a consistent four feet and did not change with the slope. The tracks also had a clear beginning and end, rather than following an existing trail. Furthermore, Johnson added that the imprints did not resemble an authentic print—for example, a human footprint shows a distinct big toe pad and typically exhibits heel slippage on a steep gradient.

What’s more, at certain points, it appeared that pine needles had been intentionally brushed aside before the track was made.

“It was obvious that the litter had been displaced sideways from the track area in an unnatural manner,” Johnson wrote. “If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail.”

From spiky seed balls to staining fruit, these ornamental trees create far more work than many homeowners anticipate...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most of us do not have unlimited free time to garden. That’s why terms like “easy-care” and “drought-tolerant” can make a shrub so appealing. And if the tree characterized as “easy-care” is also gorgeous, it has a good chance of finding its way into our garden.

But it’s important to slow down a bit and figure out if that tree is... well, if it's messy. Messy trees can be easy enough to grow, but you may be signing yourself up for relentless cleanup – and some stunning ornamentals that light up your landscape may create far more work for you than you realize.

Honestly, the messiest trees might promise the world, but they are sure to make your life infinitely more difficult, perhaps dropping spiky seed balls or spreading thousands of unwanted seedlings. And garden stores know better than to stick a “messy” label on them.

Keen to swerve the cleanup? Well, Gardening Know How is here to help!

We’ve identified six of the messiest trees around (none of which happen to be your birth month tree, thankfully) and we’re here to rat them out. We’ll outline the features of each that will win your heart, as well as what they do to earn their “messy” status, plus an equally beautiful, less messy alternative. You're welcome.

Ah the ginkgo. It’s hard to add this fabulous, ancient tree to the “messy” list given its incredible history; after all, its lineage dates back over 270 million years, and it is known as a “living fossil” because, for years, botanists believed that the tree was extinct. They found fossil evidence of its unique, fan-shaped leaves, but nary a living tree was found for years. Then, one day in the 1600s, a small grove was located in a temple garden in Japan and the world got ginkgos again.

These are wonderful, noble trees with leaves that blaze gold in the autumn. However, do not invite one into your landscape until you are assured that it is a male. Female ginkgos make the “messy” list because they drop oodles of fleshy, cherry-sized fruit that smell like rotting flesh when crushed. You’ll be cleaning up and holding your nose for a month.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Plant instead: a male gingko. There are cultivars that are all-male (like this beautiful Autumn Gold Ginkgo Tree from Nature Hills) and this is not the time to demand gender equality!

Eastern cottonwood is a messy tree with a lot to recommend it. It is a fast-growing, deciduous tree, large and impressive, sometimes reaching 150 ft tall. It plays a critical role in the ecosystem, supporting 249 caterpillar species (including your birth month caterpillar). It is also lovely, with flat leaf stems that catch even the lightest breeze, causing the heart-shaped leaves to shimmer and rustle.

But look out below! Every year a female cottonwood produces a massive volume of tiny seeds wrapped in sticky white, cotton-like fibers that blanket lawns, clog gutters, and wrap around air conditioners.

Plant instead: the Chinese pistache. If you long for a large shade tree but want to avoid cottonwood's fluffy seeds, plant a Chinese pistache like this one from Brighter Blooms. It grows more slowly and fits in well in residential gardens.

Southern magnolias are the belles of the ball in the landscape, with their goblet-shaped, intensely fragrant white blooms and large, glossy leaves. The trees are evergreens that can grow above 60 feet (20m) tall and half that wide. They have a real presence in the garden.

But don’t fall for this pretty face until you learn of the work you will be required to do to keep your garden looking good. Southern magnolia trees shed, and they shed almost constantly. They shed their heavy waxy leaves; they shed their large seed cones; and they shed spent petals. Picking up in a year-round job.

Plant instead: flowering dogwood. If you love the Southern magnolia’s showy flowers, sub in a flowering dogwood (aka the tree quietly replacing magnolias everywhere). It is a more manageable size with lovely white “flowers” that are actually bracts.

A post shared by Vikram Baliga (@the.plant.prof)

The gorgeous cloud of white spring flowers has turned many a head, and the Bradford pear (despite the controversy surrounding it) is widely used as a street tree and even in gardens. It offers a graceful, symmetrical shape, pretty spring blossoms, and lively fall foliage.

However, best enjoy looking at this little flowering tree in someone else’s yard, because those white flowers that look like they were cultivated by angels actually smell awful! Some liken the odor to rotting fish, others to sweaty foot fungus. This happens when the tree is in full bloom, and the petals hold onto the smell as they fall.

Plant instead: a wild cherry (Prunus avium). Like the Bradford pear, a cherry erupts in clusters of stunning white flowers just as spring rolls in. But something like the Montmorency Cherry Tree from Nature Hills is a native and its blossoms smell like flowers instead of fish. Those flowers produce fruit that is loved by local birds.

Oh the autumn color you’ll enjoy with a sweetgum tree! This fast-growing native tree has lovely starry leaves that turn all sorts of fiery colors before they fall. Each leaf has five to seven lobes that turn orange, crimson, and purple in autumn. A sweetgum is a tolerant tree, accepting heat, drought, and soil compaction, as well as feeding birds in winter.

But sweetgum has its downsides: primarily, the hard, spiky "gumballs" that hurt bare feet and make mowing difficult. Yes, this lovely tree drops thousands of woody seed pods from winter through spring. They hurt your feet if you walk barefoot, and even with shoes on, they can trip you up and cause ankle injuries. They even destroy lawnmower blades. Yet they are really difficult to rake up.

Plant instead: red maple (Acer rubrum). If you want a tree for fall color and shade, a seedless red maple cultivar will treat you right. It offers similar shade and a brilliant red or orange autumn display and similar shade.

What a mix! Crabapples offer spectacular spring flowers and attractive berries. They are small trees, usually under 25 feet (8m) tall, grown for their ornamental beauty and wildlife value.

However, if you get a messy crabapple variety, you may come to regret inviting the tree into your landscape. The large, juicy fruits fall readily from the tree and make the ground below a slippery mess. Having to trudge through the slippery rotting fruits is icky and even dangerous, but cleaning up cannot be called fun wither.

Plant instead: a “clean” variety of crabapple. You can select a fruitless variety like Spring Snow Crabapple (Malus 'Spring Snow'), with dense clusters of fragrant, pure white blossoms in mid-spring. Or, if you prefer, a Prairifire Flowering Crabapple Tree from Nature Hills, which promises to be far too tempting to local birds to ever spill a berry.

Of course, if you have the time to do the cleanup, then there's no harm planting a messy tree in your yard. Just be sure you're willing to roll your sleeves up and get cracking when things get mucky – and if not, one of our beautiful alternatives is definitely the better choice for you.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#8230. How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold)

My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

On November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and quickly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

As we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

The A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

As excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

At that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

Within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

Alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”

I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

Among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

The climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in big walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

The first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

When we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

At 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we quickly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

Nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

1It’s hard to guess after only one attempt, but I wouldn’t argue with 5.14a for that pitch! I also could see upper-end 5.13d, though.

#8229. Make Uphills Easier With These Exercises for Explosive Strength

Hills don’t just feel hard. Tackling steep slopes takes way more energy than walking or running at the same pace on flat ground: In fact, you burn roughly 44 percent more calories per hour walking up a 5 percent incline than on flat ground. If you’ve got that one hiking buddy who seems to power up the hills while you’re huffing and puffing, the reason isn’t just that they’re fit. It’s that they’ve built up power—specifically explosive strength, which is fitness jargon for their ability to quickly muster the strength they’ve built. Explosive strength is the same stuff you use when you jump, bound, or push yourself up a steep step.

“On every uphill stride … the first thing that happens is a very, very sharp kind of eccentric stretching load on the leg as you step up, and then you need a much higher power spike to actually get the body moving,” says Alex Viada, head coach at Complete Human Performance, and author of The Ultimate Hybrid Athlete. “If you don’t have the ability to hit those little power spikes over and over and over again, that’s a much greater determinant of uphill performance.”

Explosive strength can be trained, though. In a small 2011 study of women in their 60s and 70s published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity, one group was assigned to lift weights in a way that would build explosive strength. After 12 weeks, those women climbed stairs 17 percent faster than they did at the beginning of the study.

“Uphills are hard, and they’re hard for everyone,” says Mike Aidala, coach and owner of The Offense, a gym and mindset coaching business in Boulder, CO. He says that approaching your training with a goal of getting stronger, rather than faster, can help build uphill power.

Here’s a mental intent method from the study that can make every exercise build more explosive strength, and six specific exercises for building explosive, uphill strength from Viada, Aidala, and Rose Wetzel, a certified personal trainer and pro Spartan racer with multiple world championship podium finishes.

Explosive exercises are usually those where your body leaves the floor (like squat jumps or box jumps) or a weight leaves your hands (like medicine ball throws). But you can achieve the same benefit by performing the concentric phase—the “lift” phase—of any exercise with explosive intent. That’s how the elderly participants in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity study built power. On each repetition of machine exercises, they did the eccentric—or “lowering”—portion of the lift at a controlled pace, and then they pushed the weight up in an explosive manner.

Lifting weights in this way gives a two-way boost to your uphill performance. Not only does it build power in the “push” portion of each lift, but lowering weights slowly and under control increases the strength of your tendons.

“When we train our tendons, we’re able to be more explosive,” says Wetzel. Stronger tendons, she says, “help with the body’s ability to spring off the ground, to explode off with all that strength.”

You can use this method with almost every strength exercise you do, says Viada. His recommendation: Start with a few sets of each exercise with explosive intent, and then move into your “regular” sets of the move. During the explosive sets, he says, don’t use as much weight as you will in the later, “normal” sets.

For a starting weight, Viada suggests subtracting 25 percent from the maximum weight with which you could normally perform 10 reps. For example, if you regularly do 10 leg presses with 200 pounds, perform your explosive reps with 150 pounds.

In addition to using a lower weight, Viada also recommends doing fewer repetitions in each set. While you could probably do this weight for 15 or more repetitions, start with a handful, and make sure each one is done with maximum explosive intention.

“The only thing that matters is that they’re explosive and they’re fast,” he says. “So when you go to the bottom of the movement, think about suddenly trying to push the bar or sled up through a wall. Pretend you’re trying to smash [the weight] up through the ceiling.”

Do a few sets in this way for each move, then move to your normal, longer sets with your regular weights.

Our experts recommend these six moves to become more explosive and more stable as you trek or run uphill—they’re moves the coaches have used to train clients to climb 14ers, and that Wetzel herself has used to vault her way to multiple obstacle course race podiums.

The first four exercises can be done anywhere, including as part of a run or hike warmup. For the last two, you’ll need some gym equipment.

These jumps let you practice exploding, but also train your knee not to wobble on each step. Not only will a stable knee help prevent injuries when you’re thrown off-kilter on the trail, but will prevent you from losing energy that could be used to propel you forward.

Do one set of 10 jumps per leg three to four times per week. Over time, try to minimize wobbling, and then increase the distance of your jumps.

Similar to the previous exercise, these jumps incorporate side-to-side movement. Don’t rush through them, Aidala says. Land, get stable, take a beat, then repeat.

Do 10 jumps in each direction on each leg. Perform these three to four times per week.

These aren’t the plodding high knees you’re used to, Wetzel says.

“When I do these drills, it’s for a very short amount of time, and I do them for power,” she says. “I’m not doing high knees like someone might do for 30 seconds to get their heart rate up … it’s like six to eight seconds of hot potato, hot potato, hot potato, and then catch my breath for 30 seconds.”

You can do these before every run or hike, or as a warmup before any workout.

This move, Wetzel says, helps you to feel like you can spring off with each step up a hill. Unlike a longer jumping lunge, she does these mini lunges as quickly as possible, keeping the movement “fierce, short, and explosive.” Instead of dropping into a full lunge, bend your knees only slightly, with your feet moving front to back almost like you’re cross-country skiing while jumping slightly.

Do a few sets of 16 reps before every run, hike, or gym workout.

“Uphill running starts from the hips,” Viada says. “And with Bulgarian split squat hops, when you start that explosiveness from the bottom, you’ll explosively engage those hips like nothing else.”

This takes one of the most dreaded moves in the gym and adds an explosive element, with the front foot leaving the ground on each repetition. Your foot doesn’t need to come way off the ground, though, Viada says. An inch or so is great. Since it’s already a tough move, he recommends using a light weight, or no weight at all.

Perform three to four sets of four to five hops per leg, focusing on explosiveness in each rep. Do these two to three times per week.

When lifting with explosive intent, coaches often recommend that you “explode out of the hole,” or the bottom of the move. With the Anderson squat, you start in the hole using a squat rack, pressing the bar off pins so you can focus even more on the powerful concentric portion of the lift.

Don’t set the stops on the rack too low, Viada says. Aim so that when you get under the bar, your knees are bent 90 degrees, mimicking the angles you’ll need to hike uphill with power.

Perform three to four sets of four to five squats, focusing on explosiveness in each rep. Do these one to two times per week.
